title: lua_bin picks an interpreter with command -v, which names a non-executable file
body:
## What

`lua_bin()` in `opt/utilz/test/test_helper.bash` picks the interpreter the project's Lua suites run under by testing each candidate with `command -v`:

```
for b in lua5.4 lua luajit; do
  if command -v "$b" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    command -v "$b"
    return 0
  fi
done
```

`command -v` names a file that is present but **not executable**, which this project has already been bitten by and recorded: a non-executable hit is reported as found, and the caller then runs it and gets exit 126 or 127, which reads as the test failing rather than as the interpreter never having run.

## Measured

Found by `utilz-dc` on 10 Nov 2026 while moving this function out of `opt/arngz/test/arngz.bats` into the shared helper for ST0033, and reported to `utilz-vc`. dc deliberately kept the body identical, so the move is provable by diff, rather than smuggling a hardening into a move. That was the right call and it is why this is a separate issue.

Two suites now depend on this function: `arngz.bats`'s `AT-03.2` for `plan_test.lua`, and `engine.bats`'s `AT-01.2` for `engine_test.lua`.

## Fix

Test that the candidate is executable, not merely present, and keep the existing contract that no interpreter is a failure rather than a skip. Read 126 and 127 from a candidate as "never ran" rather than as a failing suite.

`opt/utilz/test/test_helper.bash` already has an uncommitted change in the tree from the move, so this fix costs one suite re-run rather than a second.

## Design

utilz-dc, 10 Nov 2026. Written before any code, on hv's "go with your recommendations" (utilz-vc decision 98).

### Latent, like 0136's substring

`command -v` names a non-executable file only when nothing executable of that name is on PATH: bash keeps the first existing file as a last resort. This project measured it on 16 Oct 2026 under bash 3.2.57 and 5.3.20, in the `hs` case fixed in c654d4f. On every machine that runs these suites the interpreter found is executable, so nothing is wrong today. It would bite where a non-executable `lua5.4` was the only one on PATH and an executable `lua` was also present: the old function returns the non-executable, and the suite fails with exit 126, which reads as a failing test rather than as an interpreter that never ran.

### The fix

The idiom this project already recorded for exactly this: resolve, then test.

```
for b in lua5.4 lua luajit; do
  p="$(command -v "$b" 2>/dev/null)" || continue
  if [[ "$p" != /* || -x "$p" ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "$p"
    return 0
  fi
done
return 1
```

The `!= /*` arm stops `-x` from rejecting a builtin or a function, which `command -v` prints as a bare name. None of the three candidates is one, so it changes nothing here, but it keeps the recorded idiom whole rather than a variant of it.

### Why it cannot weaken anything

Wherever the old function returned an executable, the new one returns the same path. It differs only where the old returned a non-executable, which would have failed with 126 anyway, and there it moves on to the next candidate instead. The contract is kept: no interpreter at all is still `return 1`, which the callers turn into a failure and never a skip.

The Fix above also asks that a caller read 126 and 127 as "never ran". Once `lua_bin` can return only an executable, it cannot hand a caller a 126 of its own making, so that half is subsumed here and no caller changes.

### The sibling, which is already fixed

`check_command` in `opt/utilz/lib/common.sh` has carried exactly this idiom since 2ffdc4f9 on 16 Oct 2026, for issue 0068: `p="$(command -v "$1" 2>/dev/null)" && [[ "$p" != /* || -x "$p" ]]`, at `common.sh:442`, with a comment citing the same bash 3.2.57 and 5.3.20 measurement. That is where this design's idiom comes from. An earlier wording of this section said `check_command` still carried the quirk and should be filed; that was written from a note dated before 2ffdc4f9 rather than from the code, and it was wrong. There is nothing to file.

`lua_bin` copies the idiom rather than calling `check_command`, and that is forced rather than a missed reuse: `test_helper.bash` never sources `common.sh` into a test's own shell, only into a separate `bash -c` (`run_common_strict`, and the install helpers), so `check_command` is not reachable from `lua_bin`. They are the same one-line predicate on either side of the test and runtime boundary, named here as a pair so that a change to one is a reason to look at the other.

### How it is proven

1. Both bodies, old and new, evaluated verbatim with a scratch directory holding a non-executable `lua5.4` placed first on PATH and the real interpreter after it, nothing under test running: the old body must return the non-executable and the new body must skip it and return the real interpreter. That shows both that the old was wrong and that the new is right, on a planted file in a scratch directory rather than anywhere on the real PATH.
2. The three arms that call `lua_bin`, two in `arngz.bats` and one in `engine.bats`, run green in bats in the same booked run as 0136.
